UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                         )
    Interconnection Reliability Requirements                               ) Docket No. ER26-3650-000
    for Large Loads                                                        )



     COMMENTS OF VERRUS, LLC IN SUPPORT OF MISO'S INTERCONNECTION
             RELIABILITY REQUIREMENTS FOR LARGE LOADS

         Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure1, Verrus LLC2
("Verrus") respectfully submits these comments in support of the above-captioned filing by the
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. ("MISO"), which proposes Interconnection
Reliability Requirements ("IRR") for Large Loads.3 Verrus generally supports MISO’s proposed
approach and offers the comments below to underscore that advanced, flexible computational
loads — such as those Verrus develops — can, and should, serve as active contributors to grid
reliability, not merely as loads that must be accommodated.

I. BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY OF POSITION

         MISO’s filing responds to the Commission’s June 18, 2026 order directing MISO to show
cause why its Tariff remains just and reasonable absent provisions addressing ongoing
operational requirements for large loads, including visibility, ramp rate, and disturbance
ride-through.4 MISO’s IRR Proposal seeks to establish four categories of reliability requirements
— data, modeling, telemetry, and forecasting requirements (together, “visibility”), phasor
measurement unit (“PMU”) requirements, ramp requirements, and ride-through requirements —

  18 C.F.R. § 385.213.
2
  Verrus LLC ("Verrus") is a developer, owner, and operator of a first-of-its-kind fleet of purpose-built, load-flexible
data centers designed to function not only as digital infrastructure but also as active grid assets, capable of
dynamically adjusting electricity consumption to support system reliability, efficiency, and affordability. Verrus has
been an active stakeholder participant in MISO’s Large Load Working Group ("LLWG") process addressing the
Interconnection Reliability Requirements at issue in this filing, and has separately engaged before the Commission
on large-load interconnection issues, including in Docket Nos. EL26-70-000 and RM26-4-000. Contemporaneously
with these comments, Verrus has filed a motion to intervene in this proceeding.

 scaled to a newly defined “Computational Load” subset of “Large Load,” with the more intensive
PMU, ramp, and ride-through obligations applied only to Computational Loads. 5

         Verrus supports this framework.               As explained below, Verrus (A) supports MISO’s
risk-scaled approach to applicability; (B) supports MISO’s choice to establish core obligations in
the Tariff, while reserving implementation detail to the Business Practices Manual (“BPM”) and
its ongoing stakeholder process; (C) offers its own facility design as an example demonstrating
that advanced computational loads are capable of actively supporting reliability, not merely
complying with minimum standards; (D) urges the Commission to ensure that MISO’s
Tariff-based requirements remain harmonized with the ongoing NERC standard development
effort; and (E) requests that MISO’s transition provisions continue to reasonably account for
loads still progressing toward full interconnected capacity.

II. COMMENTS

A. MISO’s Risk-Scaled Framework Reasonably Targets Requirements at the Loads That
Present Reliability Risk

         Verrus supports MISO’s determination to apply the full suite of PMU, ramp, and
ride-through requirements only to the Computational Load subset of Large Load, while applying
visibility requirements more broadly.6 This approach appropriately recognizes that not all large
loads exhibit the rapid, power-electronic-driven demand changes that motivated the
Commission’s concerns,7 and avoids imposing requirements on loads that do not present the
reliability risk those requirements are designed to address.

B. Verrus Supports Establishing Core Obligations in the Tariff While Reserving
Implementation Detail to the BPM and Stakeholder Process

          Verrus also generally supports MISO’s approach of codifying the core visibility, PMU,
ramp, and ride-through obligations in the Tariff while leaving technical details — communication
protocols, specific thresholds, and testing and demonstration procedures — to the BPM for Large

Load / Computational Load definitions).
6

while the Computational Load component of a Large Load is separately subject to PMU, ramp, and ride-through

                                                                                                                        2
 Load, which is being refined in the the continuing LLWG process.8 That approach strikes an
appropriate balance: it gives the Commission and stakeholders a clear, enforceable Tariff
framework, while preserving the flexibility MISO and stakeholders need to refine technical
requirements in a rapidly evolving area as operating experience increases.

C. Advanced Computational Loads Are Capable of Actively Supporting Grid Reliability

         Verrus’ own facility design illustrates that computational loads that would be subject to
MISO’s proposed requirements are not merely able to comply with them, but can affirmatively
support system reliability. Verrus data centers employ behind-the-meter battery energy storage
systems (“BESS”) and proprietary coordinated controls — which Verrus refers to as its
StabiliGrid™ architecture — that function as a buffer layer between the point of interconnection
and IT load, managing ramp behavior and providing sub-second ride-through support during
voltage and frequency disturbances.9 Testing and modeling of this architecture, conducted jointly
with    the    National      Laboratory       of    the    Rockies,     demonstrates        materially     reduced
point-of-interconnection power deviation during severe grid disturbances relative to the
conventional design baseline modeled in the study.10 Verrus offers this experience to illustrate
that the Commission and MISO should continue their efforts to ensure that computational loads
function as grid assets.

D. FERC Action on MISO’s Reliability Requirements Should Be Harmonized with the
Parallel NERC Standards Effort

         MISO’s own filing recognizes that its proposed ramp, PMU, and ride-through
requirements are being developed ahead of, but in alignment with, NERC’s emerging
Computational Load definition and the ongoing work of NERC’s Load Modeling Task Force.11
NERC is separately developing large-load-related reliability requirements of its own, including
through its Large Loads Task Force, Large Loads Working Group, and Project 2026-02

 (Computational Load).12         Because the MISO and NERC are advancing large-load reliability
requirements in parallel (but not in fully synchronized processes), Verrus urges the Commission,
in acting on this filing, to make clear that MISO’s Tariff-based requirements and any eventual
NERC Reliability Standard(s) addressing the same operational characteristics should be
harmonized — so that large loads such as Verrus, as well as utilities and other stakeholders, are
not left navigating duplicative, inconsistent, or conflicting obligations.

E.   MISO’s Transition Provisions Should Continue to Accommodate Loads Still
Progressing Toward Full Capacity

        Verrus supports MISO’s proposed transition provisions, which appropriately distinguish
between loads with a Service Commencement Date before the proposed effective date and those
still progressing through interconnection.13 Consistent with comments Verrus has previously
offered in the LLWG process, Verrus encourages MISO to clarify that the ramp-up process for
standards implementation accounts for the buildout period of a large load campus (which
frequently extends over several years), rather than binding at a level calibrated to initial, partial
energization.14

 III. CONCLUSION

            For the foregoing reasons, Verrus respectfully requests that the Commission accept
MISO’s filing in Docket No. ER26-3650-000, and approve MISO’s requested effective date of
December 4, 2026.15 Verrus looks forward to continuing to participate in MISO’s Large Load
Working Group as further implementation details are developed.

Respectfully submitted,

 Background
July 10, 2024: Large Load Loss Incident
On July 10, 2024 (NERC 2025), the fragility of modern load dynamics was exposed when a
lightning strike in Northern Virginia caused a transmission-level fault, lasting less than 100
milliseconds (ms), which triggered the cascading disconnection of approximately 1,500
megawatts (MW) of data center load (see Figure 1). Despite the grid fault clearing in roughly 50
ms, sensitive internal protection schemes across dozens of facilities interpreted the voltage sag as
a valid outage, transitioning information technology (IT) loads to backup power and severing
grid connection. The resulting sudden drop in demand caused a voltage swell to 1.07 p.u.,
requiring manual operator intervention to stabilize the area.

Crucially, although the facilities in Northern Virginia effectively operated within the voltage
immunity bounds of the Information Technology Industry Council (ITIC) curve, the event
exposed a fundamental misalignment: The ITIC standard is designed to protect individual server
hardware, not to maintain macro-grid stability. This resulted in the grid losing several hundred
megawatts of load almost instantaneously, creating overvoltage and oscillation.

This “near miss” has become a primary case study for North American Electric Reliability
Corporation and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) working groups, driving
new regulatory frameworks that treat data centers not just as passive customers, but as large,
dynamic loads that must possess robust voltage ride-through capabilities, adaptive protection,
and coordinated control strategies. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas recently released its
ride-through requirements (ERCOT 2025) for large electronic loads (which includes data
centers), particularly to address these types of massive load disconnection concerns.

 Current State
In practice, many data centers use disturbance-count protection that locks out after three
undervoltage events (below ~0.7–0.8 p.u.) within 60 seconds (s), transferring loads to backup
power until a manual reset is performed. In the July 10 event shown in Figure 1, the third
undervoltage (NERC 2025) triggered widespread lockouts, disconnecting approximately 1.5
gigawatts of data center load and amplifying grid instability as seen in Figure 2.




                              Figure 2. Aggregate grid load (NERC 2025)
Recently, some new data centers (Vaidhynathan et al. 2025) have incorporated commercial
battery energy storage systems (BESS) units that typically include fault ride-through and
undervoltage ride-through capabilities, as mandated by IEEE 1547 standards. However, these
responses are typically self-contained and uncoordinated with data center protection logic or
uninterruptible power supply (UPS) operation to provide a “plant-level” ride-through response.
As a result, although the BESS remains connected during short faults, it is not synchronized to
provide grid load recovery/ride-through behavior with UPS load transfer or point of
interconnection (POI) protection timing. This results in delayed power restoration and short-term
grid instability following voltage recovery persisting with conventional BESS.

This observation highlights a key gap: Existing BESS operate effectively at the device level but
lack integrated control with other critical data center assets needed for a grid-supportive response
during and after “successive” undervoltage events.

 Innovation
As data centers represent a larger percentage of overall grid load, it is increasingly critical that
they stay connected and assist the grid during short-duration grid contingencies (<~5-s) to avoid
causing wide-area outages. This is accomplished by intelligent control algorithms and/or
parameter settings for controllable assets in a data center such as IT load, cooling load, UPS,
protection settings, and distributed energy sources such as BESS and generators.

The Verrus™ StabiliGrid™ data center architecture involves four steps for data center response
that improve grid resilience:

    1. Grid contingency event detection. Uses high-resolution power quality monitoring to
       detect grid state (during events such as undervoltage, overvoltage, underfrequency, and
       overfrequency).
    2. Grid-resilient protection settings. POI settings that allow extended ride-through/grid-
       connected operation of the data center during the grid contingency, reducing the
       probability of an islanding event.
    3. Control of assets. Depending on detection of grid event, enables grid-state-driven
       autonomous dispatch of the asset to improve grid resiliency (for example, reduce power
       draw from the grid during an undervoltage event or absorb more power from the grid
       during an overvoltage event).
    4. Post-grid event response. Post-grid recovery and following a grid contingency event,
       coordinates data center assets to present firm load to the grid more quickly, similar to the
       levels before the grid contingency event.

 Results
Verrus explored the real-life incident shown in Figure 1 in its controller hardware in the loop (C-
HIL) setup at the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) to demonstrate the effectiveness of
our data center design with large-scale BESS and Verrus StabiliGrid (applicable features
described previously) in responding to the cascaded grid undervoltage events. The C-HIL setup
is developed in the Advanced Research on Integrated Energy Systems virtual emulation
environment at NLR and is based on a digital real-time simulation platform (Vaidhynathan et al.
2025).

Note although we present results from undervoltage events, the Verrus StabiliGrid design can
contribute to grid resilience during other types of short-duration grid contingencies such as
overvoltage, overfrequency, and underfrequency. Our work with NLR instantiates the previous
four-step strategy for data centers to ride through short-duration grid contingencies (~ seconds)
and provide grid support. Controllable assets used are BESS and UPS. Results from the
undervoltage grid contingency event of Figure 1 are presented in Table 1.

 Conclusion
Through this coordinated strategy implemented in Verrus StabiliGrid, the data center achieves
fault ride-through and rapid recovery for both undervoltage and overvoltage conditions without
triggering protection lockouts. The digital real-time simulations demonstrate by synchronizing
BESS, UPS, and protection logic behavior, the data center transitions from being a disturbance-
sensitive load to an active, grid-supporting participant—a key requirement for future grid-
integrated data center operations.
